slides.say: A B C is a right triangle whose sides A B and A C are tangent to a circle with center O, at B and at D. B, O, E and C lie on one straight line, and E is on the circle. Given, O E and E C are both four centimeters. What is the area of the shaded region between C D, C E and the minor arc D E, in square centimeters?
at: A B C is a right triangle

slides.say: The minor arc is the small arc between D and E. So it's a shaded-area question again. We need to decide which area to subtract from which.
at: The minor arc is the small arc

slides.say: [short pause] Let's solve it the math way. Here it isn't clear yet which areas to use. Is it the big triangle minus a few pieces? We don't know yet.
at: Let's solve it the math way

slides: So let's add the known lengths, and the radius to each touching point. That will give us a right triangle to work with.

slides.say: A B is tangent to the circle at B. B is a point of tangency, and the right angle is already marked there, because the radius O B is perpendicular to the tangent.
at: the right angle is already marked

slides.say: D is also a point of tangency, but there's no radius to it. So let's draw the radius from O to D.
That's the radius O D. A radius to a touching point is perpendicular to the tangent, so we mark the right angle at D.
How long is the radius? O E is a radius, and it's four. So O D is a radius too, and it's four.
at: So O D is a radius too

slides.say: Now we can see which areas to use. Take triangle O D C, and remove the sector D O E. What's left is exactly the shaded part. It's just like the last question.
[pause] Let's look at triangle O D C on its own, bigger. It has a right angle at D. One leg, O D, is four. The hypotenuse O C is O E plus E C, four plus four, eight.
at: Let's look at triangle O D C

slides.say: The area of a right triangle is leg times leg, over two. So we need the other leg, D C. Pythagoras would work, but here there's a quicker way.
at: is leg times leg, over two

slides.say: Look, the hypotenuse is exactly twice the leg, eight and four. That happens only in a gold triangle, the thirty, sixty, ninety triangle. So the angle opposite the short leg, at C, is thirty degrees. And the angle opposite D C, at O, is sixty degrees.
at: the hypotenuse is exactly twice the leg
So the angle opposite the short leg

slides.say: In a gold triangle, the long leg is root three times the short leg. So D C is four root three.
at: So D C is four root three

slides.say: Leg times leg, over two. Four times four root three is sixteen root three. Over two, it's eight root three.
at: Over two, it's eight root three

slides.say: [pause] Should we find the sector now? In the last question we stopped halfway and looked at the choices. Here the triangle is eight root three. We take away a sector of this circle, so its area is some number of pi. So we're looking for eight root three, minus a number of pi.
at: Should we find the sector now
Here the triangle is eight root three
So we're looking for eight root three

slides.say: Choice number two has sixteen root three, and choice number four has four root three. Neither has eight root three, so they're both out.
But this time the partial calculation doesn't finish the job. Two choices are left with eight root three, choice number one and choice number three. So we continue, and find the sector.
The sector is a part of the circle. The whole circle is pi r squared. Pi times four squared is sixteen pi.

Which part? The central angle D O E is sixty degrees. Sixty out of three hundred sixty is a sixth. A sixth of sixteen pi is sixteen pi over six. Divide the top and the bottom by two, and it's eight pi over three.
at: Sixty out of three hundred sixty
Divide the top and the bottom by two

slides.say: Choice number one has four pi over three. That's only half of our sector, so it's out. Only choice number three has both parts right, eight root three minus eight pi over three. Choice number three is our answer.
at: eight root three minus eight pi over three
Choice number three is our answer

slides.say: By the way, some students find the sector first. Then they look for something minus eight pi over three, and that rules out choice number one and choice number four. Here we need both parts, and together they leave only choice number three. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
